On Jul 7, 2016, at 12:49 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

I don’t see why the NTM would be that hard to write in Stan — it seems
like it would be a straightforward translation.  Unless I’m missing some
tricky functionality?

On Jul 7, 2016, at 12:24 AM, David Duvenaud <duve...@cs.toronto.edu> wrote:

For instance, someone implemented a neural Turing machine using autograd:
https://github.com/DoctorTeeth/diffmem/blob/master/ntm/ntm.py
Which I think would be difficult to do in Stan's modeling language.

messages.subject: Re: writing a neural Turing machine in Stan
parts:
P.S.  Dustin sent a warning:

On Jul 7, 2016, at 6:13 PM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:

NTMs are notoriously difficult to both write down and also do inference on. (a lot of tricky initialization is done and various hacks to get gradient descent to work) In principle, they can be written with the Stan math library and/or the Stan DSL. However, the practical difficulty is both how to interface with all the additional user-defined functions (and classes) written in the Stan program; and also how to enable all the inference tricks that people do for NTMs within Stan’s LBFGS optimizer.

It could be a good exercise, and it certainly emphasizes a lot of the practical difficulties. But as Daniel suggested, I suggest we aim for the digit recognition example with a typical neural network (“fully connected”) first, and then we’d have a clearer idea about getting down more complex neural network architectures and their inference in Stan.

fully-connected network to implement?

Is it as simple as letting x be data matrix, y be categorical
output z be latent parameters, and alpha and beta be coefficients
and setting:

z1 <- inv_logit(alpha * x); // first layer
z2 <- inv_logit(beta * z1); // second layer
y ~ categorical(inv_logit(z2));

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: writing a neural Turing machine in Stan
parts:
Autograd's a Python autodiff framework. So the right level
of comparison, as Dustin points out, would be building something
with our math library in C++, not with the Stan language. That
is, I think our motivations for Autograd and Stan Math are the
same---autodiffing general programs. We're working in C++,
whereas Autograd works in Python. That makes Autograd much more
accessible to most computer science researchers.

Stan's domain-specific language is at a different level of abstraction.
It's a cross-platform tool aimed at doing sampling and optimization and
variational inference in a way that's encapsulated and robust
for applied statisticians. The target audience for the language is
the same audience as for PyMC's embedded graphical model building
language and for emcee.

Stan's basic approach is more like emcee's---just build a general
density and we'll take it from there. PyMC, like
BUGS/JAGS/NIMBLE, is directed toward graphical model construction.
This graphical modeling layer is limiting, but also very useful.
By restricting models to be specified with graphical models,
there's a lot of reasoning you can do on the graphical structure
for parallelization, discrete sampling, forward sampling and
posterior predictive checking, automatic likelihood calculations
for cross-validation or WAIC, etc. etc.

I also think there's a lot of latitude for building models modularly
out of full components in something like PyMC that's lacking in Stan.
This is something I haven't seen addressed enough in the probabilistic
programming literature (please send references if you know of any).
A Stan program can include functions, but there's no way to attach another
whole model as a submodel, say as a prior, because there's a mess of global
parameter and data declarations.

The emcee package, on the other hand, is like Stan in taking a general
density as input. The really flexible thing about emcee is that
it lets you use arbitrary Python programs because it only evaluates
the density with primitive types. That makes it general enough to deal
with hairy Fortran plugins for scientific forward models (physics, energy usage,
etc.) as well as any old Python code. They use ensemble sampling methods
which don't need gradients, but also don't mix well in high dimensions.

- Bob
